annotations.text:
(Recommended) Rail D · axis: part select.
Why: the 18 sections already sit in four named parts, and the live bottom sheet earned its place by being the only pattern that shows part names on a 390 screen (round-1 rail-c-note). D keeps that advantage at the TOP of the page under the 96px header, where hardening 1b says the rail belongs, and at zero taps: with Part Four open the pill set drops from 18 to 8, so the active pill (13 Shipping) sits centred with a neighbour visible either side at 390, where round-1 Rail A showed about three of eighteen. Rail is 60px tall; every control 44px; pills are the round-1 Rail A pill unchanged.
Trade-off: moving to another part costs two taps (open the part list, pick a part) and the button must be wired with scroll-spy so the part label and pill set follow the reader; drawn only in its closed state here.

Rail E · axis: progress.
Why: the thinnest rail of the three at 48px (round-1 Rail A is 62px, D and F are 60px), and the only one whose state is legible without scrolling the rail itself: Section 13 of 18 plus a 2px clay line filled to 72.2% tells the reader where they are in an 18-section page at a glance. Both chevron buttons are 44 by 44 and the row never overflows at 390.
Trade-off: it navigates one section at a time, so reaching a far section costs up to 17 taps and the part names disappear entirely; it is a position readout more than a jump-link rail.

Rail F · axis: icon chips.
Why: a single forest-filled marker on a row of quiet white hairline chips reads as one strip instead of eighteen clay outlines, and a 16px icon gives each section a second cue at scan speed. Chips are 44px tall, 8px gaps, 60px rail.
Trade-off: the icon plus label makes each chip 100 to 140px wide, so 390 shows about three chips of eighteen (the same reach problem as Rail A) and the eighteen icons are new artwork to draw and maintain; eight of the section names have no obvious icon, which is why the drawn set leans on generic glyphs.
